 3 key steps during Medicare’s open enrollment period
 The 2027 “Medicare You” handbook was mailed to more than 70 million Medicare beneficiaries in time for the Oct. 15-Dec. 7 open enrollment period.
 The 2027 "Medicare & You" handbook (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services) More Stories At 57, Catherine Zeta-Jones targets surprises, challenges Savvy Senior: Why do women lose hair as they age? Are there actually health benefits to eating an apple a day? Before saying yes to a medical test, know the risks and benefits 
 By Toni King Toni Says 
 October 22, 2026 - 5:30 am 
 Dear Toni: I enrolled in Medicare in 2025 but have not received my 2027 “Medicare &You” handbook, and I’m concerned about what I should do during the fall Medicare season. I have health problems, and I might make the wrong change to my Medicare or prescription drug plan.
 I am stressed by the marketing materials I am receiving from insurance plans, especially from Medicare Advantage companies. I would really appreciate any advice you can give me since Medicare season has started. — Jeff, Las Vegas
 Dear Jeff: Take your time researching your Medicare options because of your health issues. The 2027 “Medicare &You” handbook was mailed to more than 70 million Medicare beneficiaries to arrive before Oct. 1, in time for the Oct. 15-Dec. 7 open enrollment period.
 If you did not receive your copy, you can request one by calling 800-MEDICARE (633-4227) or access the handbook online at Medicare.gov.
 Here are three steps that the Toni Says team follows when helping clients during Medicare’s open enrollment period:
 Decide whether you want original Medicare (Parts A and B) or a Medicare Advantage (Part C) plan. 
 Ask your doctor’s office which plan it recommends. Most doctors accept original Medicare, but not all accept Medicare Advantage HMO or PPO plans. If your doctor is in a Medicare Advantage plan’s provider directory, be sure to verify that physician will still be accepting the plan next year. This cannot be stressed enough.
 The main difference between these two types of coverage: Original Medicare is administered by Medicare, often with a supplemental or Medigap policy that covers deductibles or coinsurances. Medicare Advantage plans are administered by private insurance companies that are approved by Medicare.
 Decide whether you need to enroll in or change your current Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage. 
 If you want Medicare prescription drug coverage to go with original Medicare, you must enroll in a stand-alone Part D plan, which may have a monthly premium.
 If you choose a Medicare Advantage plan, make sure it includes Part D plan to avoid a penalty for not enrolling in prescription drug coverage.
 Whichever plan you choose, verify that all of your prescriptions are covered under its formulary.
 Don’t forget: You have until midnight Dec. 7 to enroll in a new Part D plan for coverage to begin Jan. 1. 
 Toni King writes about Medicare and health insurance issues. If you have a question, email info@tonisays.com or call 832-519-8664.
